claim: TRPM2 is a cation channel important for the immune response, insulin secretion, and body temperature regulation.
source: Transient Receptor Potential Melastatin 2 (TRPM2) is a cation channel important for the immune response, insulin secretion, and body temperature regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about TRPM2 function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: TRPM2 is activated by cytosolic ADP ribose (ADPR).
source: It is activated by cytosolic ADP ribose (ADPR) and contains a nudix-type motif 9 (NUDT9)-homology (NUDT9-H) domain homologous to ADPR phosphohydrolases (ADPRases).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is established knowledge about TRPM2 activation.

claim: TRPM2 contains a NUDT9-homology (NUDT9-H) domain homologous to ADPR phosphohydrolases (ADPRases).
source: It is activated by cytosolic ADP ribose (ADPR) and contains a nudix-type motif 9 (NUDT9)-homology (NUDT9-H) domain homologous to ADPR phosphohydrolases (ADPRases).
evidence: This is a structural description of TRPM2 based on sequence homology, which is established knowledge.

claim: Human TRPM2 (hsTRPM2) is catalytically inactive due to mutations in the conserved Nudix box sequence.
source: Human TRPM2 (hsTRPM2) is catalytically inactive due to mutations in the conserved Nudix box sequence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work (Iordanov et al., 2016) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: TRPM2 Nudix motifs are canonical in all invertebrates but vestigial in vertebrates.
source: Here, we show that TRPM2 Nudix motifs are canonical in all invertebrates but vestigial in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TRPM2 of the cnidarian Nematostella vectensis (nvTRPM2) is an active ADPRase.
source: Correspondingly, TRPM2 of the cnidarian Nematostella vectensis (nvTRPM2) and the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta (srTRPM2) are active ADPRases.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: TRPM2 of the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta (srTRPM2) is an active ADPRase.
source: Correspondingly, TRPM2 of the cnidarian Nematostella vectensis (nvTRPM2) and the choanoflagellate Salpingoeca rosetta (srTRPM2) are active ADPRases.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic activity assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Disruption of ADPRase activity fails to affect nvTRPM2 channel currents.
source: Disruption of ADPRase activity fails to affect nvTRPM2 channel currents, reporting a catalytic cycle uncoupled from gating.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data shown in Figures 4-7 where mutations and conditions that abolish enzymatic activity do not affect channel gating.

claim: The catalytic cycle of nvTRPM2 is uncoupled from gating.
source: Disruption of ADPRase activity fails to affect nvTRPM2 channel currents, reporting a catalytic cycle uncoupled from gating.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data showing that disrupting catalysis does not affect channel function.

claim: Pore sequence substitutions responsible for inactivation of hsTRPM2 appeared in vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, pore sequence substitutions responsible for inactivation of hsTRPM2 also appeared in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) TRPM2 (drTRPM2) channels inactivate.
source: Correspondingly, zebrafish (Danio rerio) TRPM2 (drTRPM2) and hsTRPM2 channels inactivate, but srTRPM2 and nvTRPM2 currents are stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional recordings shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Human TRPM2 (hsTRPM2) channels inactivate.
source: Correspondingly, zebrafish (Danio rerio) TRPM2 (drTRPM2) and hsTRPM2 channels inactivate, but srTRPM2 and nvTRPM2 currents are stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional recordings shown in Figure 8E and is also established knowledge from prior work.

claim: srTRPM2 currents are stable.
source: Correspondingly, zebrafish (Danio rerio) TRPM2 (drTRPM2) and hsTRPM2 channels inactivate, but srTRPM2 and nvTRPM2 currents are stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional recordings shown in Figure 8B.

claim: nvTRPM2 currents are stable.
source: Correspondingly, zebrafish (Danio rerio) TRPM2 (drTRPM2) and hsTRPM2 channels inactivate, but srTRPM2 and nvTRPM2 currents are stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional recordings shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Catalysis and pore stability were lost simultaneously in vertebrate TRPM2 channels.
source: Thus, catalysis and pore stability were lost simultaneously in vertebrate TRPM2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined sequence and functional data showing that both features changed between invertebrates and vertebrates.

claim: TRPM2 channels are expressed in immune cells, pancreatic beta cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons in the brain.
source: The Transient Receptor Potential Melastatin 2 (TRPM2) protein forms Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channels that are expressed in immune cells, pancreatic beta cells, cardiomyocytes, and neurons in the brain (Nagamine et al., 1998; Perraud et al., 2001; Togashi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TRPM2 channels become activated under conditions of oxidative stress.
source: TRPM2 channels become activated under conditions of oxidative stress (Hara et al., 2002) and contribute to the Ca2+ influx that triggers insulin secretion (Uchida et al., 2011), immune cell activation (Yamamoto et al., 2008), and heat responses of heat sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus responsible for body temperature regulation (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hara et al., 2002.

claim: TRPM2 contributes to Ca2+ influx that triggers insulin secretion.
source: TRPM2 channels become activated under conditions of oxidative stress (Hara et al., 2002) and contribute to the Ca2+ influx that triggers insulin secretion (Uchida et al., 2011), immune cell activation (Yamamoto et al., 2008), and heat responses of heat sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus responsible for body temperature regulation (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Uchida et al., 2011.

claim: TRPM2 contributes to immune cell activation.
source: TRPM2 channels become activated under conditions of oxidative stress (Hara et al., 2002) and contribute to the Ca2+ influx that triggers insulin secretion (Uchida et al., 2011), immune cell activation (Yamamoto et al., 2008), and heat responses of heat sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus responsible for body temperature regulation (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yamamoto et al., 2008.

claim: TRPM2 contributes to heat responses of heat sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus responsible for body temperature regulation.
source: TRPM2 channels become activated under conditions of oxidative stress (Hara et al., 2002) and contribute to the Ca2+ influx that triggers insulin secretion (Uchida et al., 2011), immune cell activation (Yamamoto et al., 2008), and heat responses of heat sensitive neurons in the preoptic area of the hypothalamus responsible for body temperature regulation (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Song et al., 2016.

claim: Ca2+ influx through TRPM2 channels contributes to neuronal cell death following brain ischemia and in certain neurodegenerative diseases.
source: On the other hand, Ca2+ influx through TRPM2 channels contributes to neuronal cell death following brain ischemia and in certain neurodegenerative diseases (Hara et al., 2002; Kaneko et al., 2006; Fonfria et al., 2005; Hermosura et al., 2008; McQuillin et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: TRPM2 has become an attractive pharmacological target for treating chronic inflammatory diseases, diabetes, congenital hyperinsulinism, excessive fever, and neuronal cell death following stroke.
source: Thus, TRPM2 has become an attractive pharmacological target for treating chronic inflammatory diseases, diabetes, congenital hyperinsulinism, excessive fever, and neuronal cell death following stroke.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pathological roles of TRPM2 described in the preceding sentences.

claim: Each subunit of a homotetrameric TRPM2 channel is formed by ~1500 amino acid residues.
source: Each subunit of a homotetrameric TRPM2 channel is formed by ~1500 amino acid residues that are organized into a large cytosolic N-terminal region, a pore forming transmembrane region with a topology typical to voltage-gated cation channels, and a cytosolic C-terminal region.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about TRPM2.

claim: The NUDT9-H domain is an ~270 amino acid domain in the C-terminal region of TRPM2.
source: In the C-terminal region, the conserved TRP helices and coiled-coil region are followed by an ~270 amino acid domain termed NUDT9-H, for homology with the soluble mitochondrial enzyme NUDT9 (Perraud et al., 2001), an ADP-ribose (ADPR) hydrolase (ADPRase) which splits ADPR into AMP and ribose-5-phosphate (Perraud et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citations.

claim: NUDT9 is an ADP-ribose (ADPR) hydrolase (ADPRase) which splits ADPR into AMP and ribose-5-phosphate.
source: In the C-terminal region, the conserved TRP helices and coiled-coil region are followed by an ~270 amino acid domain termed NUDT9-H, for homology with the soluble mitochondrial enzyme NUDT9 (Perraud et al., 2001), an ADP-ribose (ADPR) hydrolase (ADPRase) which splits ADPR into AMP and ribose-5-phosphate (Perraud et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perraud et al., 2003.

claim: TRPM2 channels are co-activated by binding of cytosolic ADPR and Ca2+.
source: TRPM2 channels are co-activated by binding of cytosolic ADPR and Ca2+ (McHugh et al., 2003; Csanády and Törocsik, 2009), but their activity also requires the presence of phosphatydil-inositol-bisphosphate (PIP2) in the membrane (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TRPM2 channel activity requires the presence of phosphatydil-inositol-bisphosphate (PIP2) in the membrane.
source: TRPM2 channels are co-activated by binding of cytosolic ADPR and Ca2+ (McHugh et al., 2003; Csanády and Törocsik, 2009), but their activity also requires the presence of phosphatydil-inositol-bisphosphate (PIP2) in the membrane (Tóth and Csanády, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tóth and Csanády, 2012.

claim: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 binds ADPR.
source: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 binds ADPR (Grubisha et al., 2006) but is enzymatically inactive (Iordanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grubisha et al., 2006.

claim: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 is enzymatically inactive.
source: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 binds ADPR (Grubisha et al., 2006) but is enzymatically inactive (Iordanov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Iordanov et al., 2016.

claim: ADPRase enzymes belong to the large family of Nudix hydrolases that harbor a highly conserved 'Nudix box' sequence.
source: ADPRase enzymes belong to the large family of Nudix (nucleoside diphosphate linked moiety X) hydrolases that harbor a highly conserved 'Nudix box' sequence (consensus: REUXEE, U = hydrophobic) at the heart of a more extended 'Nudix motif' (Mildvan et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mildvan et al., 2005.

claim: The consensus Nudix box sequence is REUXEE (U = hydrophobic).
source: ADPRase enzymes belong to the large family of Nudix (nucleoside diphosphate linked moiety X) hydrolases that harbor a highly conserved 'Nudix box' sequence (consensus: REUXEE, U = hydrophobic) at the heart of a more extended 'Nudix motif' (Mildvan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nudix enzymes supported by citation.

claim: In the structure of mitochondrial NUDT9 protein, the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate in the Nudix box participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site.
source: In the structure of the mitochondrial NUDT9 protein (Nudix box: REFGEE), the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate (underlined) are both seen to participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site, and the first glutamate is also involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion (Shen et al., 2003); mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive (Perraud et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2003), just as the NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 (Iordanov et al., 2016) which lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate (Nudix box: RILRQE).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2003 describing the NUDT9 structure.

claim: The first conserved glutamate in the Nudix box of NUDT9 is involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion.
source: In the structure of the mitochondrial NUDT9 protein (Nudix box: REFGEE), the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate (underlined) are both seen to participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site, and the first glutamate is also involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion (Shen et al., 2003); mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive (Perraud et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2003), just as the NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 (Iordanov et al., 2016) which lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate (Nudix box: RILRQE).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shen et al., 2003.

claim: Mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive.
source: In the structure of the mitochondrial NUDT9 protein (Nudix box: REFGEE), the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate (underlined) are both seen to participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site, and the first glutamate is also involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion (Shen et al., 2003); mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive (Perraud et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2003), just as the NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 (Iordanov et al., 2016) which lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate (Nudix box: RILRQE).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perraud et al., 2003 and Shen et al., 2003.

claim: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 has a Nudix box sequence of RILRQE.
source: In the structure of the mitochondrial NUDT9 protein (Nudix box: REFGEE), the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate (underlined) are both seen to participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site, and the first glutamate is also involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion (Shen et al., 2003); mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive (Perraud et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2003), just as the NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 (Iordanov et al., 2016) which lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate (Nudix box: RILRQE).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the sequence of human TRPM2.

claim: The NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate.
source: In the structure of the mitochondrial NUDT9 protein (Nudix box: REFGEE), the side chains of the first and third conserved glutamate (underlined) are both seen to participate in the formation of salt bridges that stabilize the active site, and the first glutamate is also involved in the coordination of a catalytic Mg2+ ion (Shen et al., 2003); mutant NUDT9 proteins with RILGEE or REFGKK Nudix box sequences are inactive (Perraud et al., 2003; Shen et al., 2003), just as the NUDT9-H domain of human TRPM2 (Iordanov et al., 2016) which lacks the Mg2+ coordinating glutamate (Nudix box: RILRQE).
evidence: This is an inference based on the sequence comparison showing that the first glutamate is replaced by isoleucine in human TRPM2.

claim: Recent electron-cryomicroscopy structures of sea anemone, zebrafish, and human TRPM2 revealed an overall organization similar to that of other TRPM family channels.
source: Recent electron-cryomicroscopy structures of sea anemone (Zhang et al., 2018), zebrafish (Huang et al., 2018), and human (Wang et al., 2018) TRPM2 revealed an overall organization similar to that of other TRPM family channels in which the N-terminal regions, together with the C-terminal TRP and coiled-coil helices, assemble into a two-layered cytosolic structure below the transmembrane domain (e.g. Autzen et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2017; Winkler et al., 2017; Yin et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: In the zebrafish and human TRPM2 structures, an additional cytosolic layer formed by the four NUDT9-H domains is clearly resolved.
source: In the zebrafish and human TRPM2 structures, an additional cytosolic layer formed by the four NUDT9-H domains is clearly resolved (Huang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the zebrafish and human TRPM2 structures.

claim: TRPM2 channels from the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis remain activatable by ADPR following deletion of the NUDT9-H domain.
source: Interestingly, TRPM2 channels from the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis (nvTRPM2) remain activatable by ADPR following deletion of the NUDT9-H domain, suggesting the presence of an additional ADPR binding site (Kühn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kühn et al., 2016.

claim: nvTRPM2 has an additional ADPR binding site beyond the NUDT9-H domain.
source: Interestingly, TRPM2 channels from the sea anemone Nematostella vectensis (nvTRPM2) remain activatable by ADPR following deletion of the NUDT9-H domain, suggesting the presence of an additional ADPR binding site (Kühn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that deletion of NUDT9-H does not abolish ADPR activation.

claim: In the ADPR-bound structure of zebrafish TRPM2, a clear density for a bound ADPR molecule is seen in a cleft formed by the first N-terminal domain.
source: Correspondingly, in the ADPR-bound structure of zebrafish TRPM2, a clear density for a bound ADPR molecule is seen in a cleft formed by the first N-terminal domain (the 'N-terminal site').
evidence: This claim is based on structural data from the zebrafish TRPM2 structure.

claim: Due to limited resolution, the presence of ADPR bound to the NUDT9-H domain could not be confirmed in the zebrafish or human TRPM2 structures.
source: Although due to limited resolution the presence of ADPR bound to the NUDT9-H domain could be confirmed neither in the zebrafish nor in the human structure, in both structures pore opening was seen to be coupled to large conformational rearrangements of the four NUDT9-H domains.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the structural data.

claim: In zebrafish and human TRPM2 structures, pore opening was seen to be coupled to large conformational rearrangements of the four NUDT9-H domains.
source: Although due to limited resolution the presence of ADPR bound to the NUDT9-H domain could be confirmed neither in the zebrafish nor in the human structure, in both structures pore opening was seen to be coupled to large conformational rearrangements of the four NUDT9-H domains.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparisons from the cited studies.

claim: Channel activity of zebrafish TRPM2 was diminished by mutations in the N-terminal ADPR binding site.
source: Moreover, channel activity was diminished by mutations in the N-terminal site in zebrafish, but not human, TRPM2, whereas it was abolished for both proteins by deletion of the NUDT9-H domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from the cited studies.

claim: Channel activity of human TRPM2 was not diminished by mutations in the N-terminal ADPR binding site.
source: Moreover, channel activity was diminished by mutations in the N-terminal site in zebrafish, but not human, TRPM2, whereas it was abolished for both proteins by deletion of the NUDT9-H domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from the cited studies.

claim: Channel activity was abolished for both zebrafish and human TRPM2 by deletion of the NUDT9-H domain.
source: Moreover, channel activity was diminished by mutations in the N-terminal site in zebrafish, but not human, TRPM2, whereas it was abolished for both proteins by deletion of the NUDT9-H domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by functional data from the cited studies.

claim: The Nudix box sequences are canonical for all invertebrate TRPM2 proteins.
source: Interestingly, the Nudix box sequences are canonical for all invertebrate TRPM2 proteins, but their enzymatic activities have never been directly tested.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The enzymatic activities of invertebrate TRPM2 proteins have never been directly tested prior to this study.
source: Interestingly, the Nudix box sequences are canonical for all invertebrate TRPM2 proteins, but their enzymatic activities have never been directly tested.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature prior to this work.

claim: Deletion or mutations of the NUDT9-H domain sensitized nvTRPM2 currents toward activation by H2O2 in intact cells.
source: In intact cells, deletion or mutations of the NUDT9-H domain sensitized nvTRPM2 currents toward activation by H2O2, which was interpreted to reflect ADPRase activity of the intact protein (Kühn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kühn et al., 2016.

claim: Full-length nvTRPM2 protein shows robust ADPRase activity.
source: The purified nvTRPM2 protein showed robust ADPRase activity, characterized by a KM of 18 ± 2 μM (Figure 2A, black symbols and fit line) and a kcat of 41 ± 2 s−1/subunit (Figure 2B, black bar), establishing nvTRPM2 as a true chanzyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 2.

claim: nvTRPM2 has a KM for ADPR of 18 ± 2 μM.
source: The purified nvTRPM2 protein showed robust ADPRase activity, characterized by a KM of 18 ± 2 μM (Figure 2A, black symbols and fit line) and a kcat of 41 ± 2 s−1/subunit (Figure 2B, black bar), establishing nvTRPM2 as a true chanzyme.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: nvTRPM2 has a kcat of 41 ± 2 s−1/subunit.
source: The purified nvTRPM2 protein showed robust ADPRase activity, characterized by a KM of 18 ± 2 μM (Figure 2A, black symbols and fit line) and a kcat of 41 ± 2 s−1/subunit (Figure 2B, black bar), establishing nvTRPM2 as a true chanzyme.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: nvTRPM2 is a true chanzyme.
source: The purified nvTRPM2 protein showed robust ADPRase activity, characterized by a KM of 18 ± 2 μM (Figure 2A, black symbols and fit line) and a kcat of 41 ± 2 s−1/subunit (Figure 2B, black bar), establishing nvTRPM2 as a true chanzyme.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstration of both channel and enzymatic activities.

claim: Isolated nvNUDT9-H displays robust ADPRase activity with a KM of 7.7 ± 1.4 μM.
source: When assayed under similar conditions as the full-length protein, nvNUDT9-H displayed similarly robust ADPRase activity, with a somewhat lower KM (7.7 ± 1.4 μM; Figure 2A, green symbols and fit line) but a nearly identical kcat value (40 ± 3 s−1; Figure 2B, green bar).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Isolated nvNUDT9-H has a kcat value of 40 ± 3 s−1.
source: When assayed under similar conditions as the full-length protein, nvNUDT9-H displayed similarly robust ADPRase activity, with a somewhat lower KM (7.7 ± 1.4 μM; Figure 2A, green symbols and fit line) but a nearly identical kcat value (40 ± 3 s−1; Figure 2B, green bar).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Isolated nvNUDT9-H provides a convenient model system to study nvTRPM2 catalytic properties.
source: Thus, although an additional binding site for ADPR is likely formed by the N-terminal domains also in nvTRPM2 (Kühn et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018), hydrolysis of ADPR is mediated by the NUDT9-H domain which, when expressed in isolation, provides a convenient model system to study nvTRPM2 catalytic properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the similar catalytic properties of the isolated domain and full-length protein.

claim: Nudix-family enzymes require the presence of Mg2+ ions and basic pH for maximal activity.
source: Because Nudix-family enzymes require the presence of Mg2+ ions and basic pH for maximal activity (Perraud et al., 2003; Mildvan et al., 2005; Iordanov et al., 2016), the assay was done at pH = 8.0, in the presence of 10 mM Mg2+.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Nudix enzymes supported by citations.

claim: At all pH values, kcat of nvNUDT9-H was a saturable function of free [Mg2+].
source: At all pH values, kcat was a saturable function of free [Mg2+] (Figure 2C, colored symbols), but fits to the Hill equation (Figure 2C, colored curves) reported a progressive reduction in maximal kcat (kcat,max), and a progressive increase in K1/2, at lower pH values (from kcat,max = 43.9 ± 1.9 s−1 and K1/2 = 1.6 ± 0.2 mM at pH 8.5 (black curve) to kcat,max = 3.5 ± 0.6 s−1 and K1/2 = 10.8 ± 3.5 mM at pH 5.7 (red curve)).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The apparent Hill coefficient for Mg2+ binding to nvNUDT9-H remained ~2 regardless of pH.
source: On the other hand, the apparent Hill coefficient remained ~2 regardless of pH, suggesting the involvement of at least two Mg2+ ions in ADPR coordination in the active site, as observed in structures of other ADPRases (Gabelli et al., 2002; Shen et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and comparison to other ADPRase structures.

claim: At least two Mg2+ ions are involved in ADPR coordination in the active site of nvNUDT9-H.
source: On the other hand, the apparent Hill coefficient remained ~2 regardless of pH, suggesting the involvement of at least two Mg2+ ions in ADPR coordination in the active site, as observed in structures of other ADPRases (Gabelli et al., 2002; Shen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hill coefficient of ~2 and comparison to other ADPRase structures.

claim: At any fixed [Mg2+], pH-dependence of kcat for nvNUDT9-H was well described by titration of a single group.
source: In contrast, at any fixed [Mg2+], pH-dependence of kcat (Figure 2D, symbols) was well described by titration of a single group (Figure 2D, curves), suggesting a key role in catalysis of a protonatable side chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A protonatable side chain plays a key role in catalysis by nvNUDT9-H.
source: In contrast, at any fixed [Mg2+], pH-dependence of kcat (Figure 2D, symbols) was well described by titration of a single group (Figure 2D, curves), suggesting a key role in catalysis of a protonatable side chain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-dependence data.

claim: The catalytically important protonatable side chain in nvNUDT9-H is likely near the bound Mg2+ ion(s).
source: Furthermore, based on the sensitivity of its apparent pKa value to free [Mg2+] (Figure 2D, red vs. blue curve), that side chain is likely near the bound Mg2+ ion(s).
evidence: This is an inference based on the Mg2+-dependence of the apparent pKa.

claim: Purified srNUDT9-H protein displays clear ADPRase activity.
source: Indeed, the purified srNUDT9-H protein also displayed clear ADPRase activity, with a KM value (5.9 ± 0.7 μM; Figure 3A, black symbols and fit line) similar to that of nvNUDT9-H, but a kcat value of only ~2 s−1 in 1–10 mM Mg2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: srNUDT9-H has a KM value of 5.9 ± 0.7 μM for ADPR.
source: Indeed, the purified srNUDT9-H protein also displayed clear ADPRase activity, with a KM value (5.9 ± 0.7 μM; Figure 3A, black symbols and fit line) similar to that of nvNUDT9-H, but a kcat value of only ~2 s−1 in 1–10 mM Mg2+.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: srNUDT9-H has a kcat value of ~2 s−1 in 1–10 mM Mg2+.
source: Indeed, the purified srNUDT9-H protein also displayed clear ADPRase activity, with a KM value (5.9 ± 0.7 μM; Figure 3A, black symbols and fit line) similar to that of nvNUDT9-H, but a kcat value of only ~2 s−1 in 1–10 mM Mg2+.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays.

claim: Fitting the [Mg2+] dependence of kcat for srNUDT9-H required postulation of high- and low-affinity Mg2+ binding sites.
source: At both pH 8.5 and 7.1, fitting the [Mg2+] dependence of kcat (Figure 3B, black and green symbols) required postulation of high- and low-affinity Mg2+ binding sites.
evidence: This claim is based on the fitting of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The apparent Hill coefficient for the high-affinity Mg2+ site in srNUDT9-H is ~2.
source: Fits to a double Hill-curve (Figure 3B, solid curves) returned an apparent Hill coefficient of ~2 for the high-affinity site and ~1 for the low-affinity site, suggesting high-affinity binding of two Mg2+ ions to be required for catalysis, but further enhancement of kcat through low-affinity binding of a third Mg2+.
evidence: This is a result from fitting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The apparent Hill coefficient for the low-affinity Mg2+ site in srNUDT9-H is ~1.
source: Fits to a double Hill-curve (Figure 3B, solid curves) returned an apparent Hill coefficient of ~2 for the high-affinity site and ~1 for the low-affinity site, suggesting high-affinity binding of two Mg2+ ions to be required for catalysis, but further enhancement of kcat through low-affinity binding of a third Mg2+.
evidence: This is a result from fitting data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: High-affinity binding of two Mg2+ ions is required for catalysis by srNUDT9-H.
source: Fits to a double Hill-curve (Figure 3B, solid curves) returned an apparent Hill coefficient of ~2 for the high-affinity site and ~1 for the low-affinity site, suggesting high-affinity binding of two Mg2+ ions to be required for catalysis, but further enhancement of kcat through low-affinity binding of a third Mg2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hill coefficient of ~2 for the high-affinity site.

claim: Low-affinity binding of a third Mg2+ further enhances kcat of srNUDT9-H.
source: Fits to a double Hill-curve (Figure 3B, solid curves) returned an apparent Hill coefficient of ~2 for the high-affinity site and ~1 for the low-affinity site, suggesting high-affinity binding of two Mg2+ ions to be required for catalysis, but further enhancement of kcat through low-affinity binding of a third Mg2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of a low-affinity Mg2+ binding site.

claim: K1/2 of the high-affinity Mg2+ site in srNUDT9-H is sensitive to pH.
source: Similarly to nvTRPM2, K1/2 of the high-affinity Mg2+ site in srNUDT9-H was sensitive to pH (K1/2 was 0.031 ± 0.002 mM at pH = 8.5 but 0.102 ± 0.008 mM at pH 7.1), consistent with the presence of a protonatable side chain near the bound Mg2+ ions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A protonatable side chain is present near the bound Mg2+ ions in srNUDT9-H.
source: Similarly to nvTRPM2, K1/2 of the high-affinity Mg2+ site in srNUDT9-H was sensitive to pH (K1/2 was 0.031 ± 0.002 mM at pH = 8.5 but 0.102 ± 0.008 mM at pH 7.1), consistent with the presence of a protonatable side chain near the bound Mg2+ ions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-sensitivity of the K1/2 for the high-affinity Mg2+ site.

claim: Mg2+ binding to the low-affinity site in srNUDT9-H is insensitive to pH.
source: In contrast, Mg2+ binding to the low-affinity site was insensitive to pH (K1/2~30 mM), suggesting that this site is further away from the catalytically important titratable side chain.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The low-affinity Mg2+ binding site in srNUDT9-H is further away from the catalytically important titratable side chain.
source: In contrast, Mg2+ binding to the low-affinity site was insensitive to pH (K1/2~30 mM), suggesting that this site is further away from the catalytically important titratable side chain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pH-insensitivity of the low-affinity site.

claim: Full-length srTRPM2 has a kcat value (lower estimate) of ~1.6 s−1/subunit under conditions of pH 8.5 and 16 mM [Mg2+].
source: Nevertheless, tentative ADPRase assays using freshly isolated full-length srTRPM2 revealed a kcat value (lower estimate) of ~1.6 s−1/subunit (Figure 3C, brown bar), comparable to that obtained for isolated srNUDT9-H (Figure 3C, black bar) under identical conditions (pH 8.5, 16 mM [Mg2+]).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from enzymatic assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ADPRase activity is a shared feature of invertebrate TRPM2 proteins.
source: Thus, despite species-specific differences in its precise catalytic mechanism, ADPRase activity seems to be a shared feature of invertebrate TRPM2 proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the demonstration of ADPRase activity in both nvTRPM2 and srTRPM2.

claim: In CFTR, ATP hydrolysis cycles at cytosolic nucleotide-binding domains are strictly coupled to conformational changes that open and close the channel pore.
source: In CFTR, ATP hydrolysis cycles at cytosolic nucleotide-binding domains are strictly coupled to conformational changes that open and close (gate) the channel pore (Csanády et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Csanády et al., 2010.

claim: The catalytic activity of the cytosolic kinase domain in TRPM6/7 is not linked to gating conformational changes of those channels.
source: In contrast, the catalytic activity of the cytosolic kinase domain in TRPM6/7 is not linked to gating conformational changes of those channels (Krapivinsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Krapivinsky et al., 2014.

claim: Comparison of ligand-free, closed, and ADPR+Ca2+-bound, open, conformations of zebrafish and human TRPM2 suggested large movements of the four NUDT9-H domains upon opening of ADPR-bound channels.
source: Comparison of the ligand-free, closed, and ADPR+Ca2+-bound, open, conformations of zebrafish and human TRPM2 suggested large movements of the four NUDT9-H domains upon opening of ADPR-bound channels.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparisons from cited studies.

claim: Large movements of NUDT9-H domains appear to stabilize the open state of TRPM2 channels.
source: These rearrangements appear to stabilize the open state (Huang et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018), suggesting a potential influence of NUDT9-H ligand-occupancy on channel gating.
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis from cited studies.

claim: Omission of Mg2+ from the reaction buffer abolished ADPRase activity of nvNUDT9-H to below the limit of detection.
source: Consistent with the exquisite Mg2+ dependence of nvNUDT9-H catalysis (Figure 2C), omission of Mg2+ from the reaction buffer with or without additon of 100 μM CDTA (free [Mg2+] low nanomolar and low micromolar, respectively) abolished ADPRase activity of the protein to below the limit of detection of our assay (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Removal of cytosolic Mg2+ increased nvTRPM2 macroscopic currents almost twofold.
source: Interestingly, currents activated in the absence of cytosolic Mg2+ were almost twofold larger (Figure 4B; Figure 4C, left pair of bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The increase in nvTRPM2 macroscopic current upon Mg2+ removal reflected a similar fold increase in unitary current amplitude.
source: However, this effect reflected a similarfold increase in unitary current amplitude (Figure 4C, right pair of bars), from ~−2.5 pA to ~−4 pA at −20 mV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), rather than a change in channel open probability: in the presence of cytosolic Mg2+, at −20 mV membrane potential, Na+ influx through open nvTRPM2 channel pores is blocked by cytosolic Mg2+ ions.
evidence: This claim is supported by unitary current measurements shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of cytosolic Mg2+, at −20 mV membrane potential, Na+ influx through open nvTRPM2 channel pores is blocked by cytosolic Mg2+ ions.
source: However, this effect reflected a similarfold increase in unitary current amplitude (Figure 4C, right pair of bars), from ~−2.5 pA to ~−4 pA at −20 mV (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), rather than a change in channel open probability: in the presence of cytosolic Mg2+, at −20 mV membrane potential, Na+ influx through open nvTRPM2 channel pores is blocked by cytosolic Mg2+ ions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unitary current data explaining the mechanism of Mg2+ block.

claim: The time constants of nvTRPM2 channel deactivation upon sudden removal of cytosolic ADPR were not measurably prolonged by Mg2+ removal.
source: Moreover, the time constants of channel deactivation upon sudden removal of cytosolic ADPR (Figure 4B, colored numbers, in ms), obtained from single-exponential fits (colored lines) was not measurably prolonged by Mg2+ removal (Figure 4D), as would be expected if ADPR hydrolysis facilitated pore closure.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis of deactivation shown in Figure 4B and 4D.

claim: Removal of cytosolic Mg2+ disrupts catalytic activity at the nvNUDT9-H domain but does not affect macroscopic gating parameters of nvTRPM2 channels.
source: Thus, while removal of cytosolic Mg2+ disrupts catalytic activity at the nvNUDT9-H domain, it does not affect macroscopic gating parameters of nvTRPM2 channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined enzymatic and electrophysiological data.

claim: AMPCPR is resistant to hydrolysis by nvNUDT9-H.
source: Correspondingly, whereas the slow spontaneous hydrolysis of ADPR was accelerated by nvNUDT9-H to an extent roughly proportional to the concentration of the enzyme (Figure 5A, bars 2, 5, and 7), AMPCPR showed no sign of spontaneous hydrolysis, and remained unhydrolyzed in the presence of increasing amounts of nvNUDT9-H protein (Figure 5A, bars 3, 6, and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AMPCPR readily activated nvTRPM2 channel currents.
source: On the other hand, AMPCPR readily activated nvTRPM2 channel currents, although, compared to ADPR, higher (tens of micromolar) concentrations of the analog were required.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Higher concentrations of AMPCPR are required to activate nvTRPM2 compared to ADPR.
source: On the other hand, AMPCPR readily activated nvTRPM2 channel currents, although, compared to ADPR, higher (tens of micromolar) concentrations of the analog were required.
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Even in the presence of a quasi-saturating concentration of AMPCPR, nvTRPM2 currents remained smaller than in 100 μM ADPR.
source: Moreover, even in the presence of a quasi-saturating concentration of AMPCPR, currents remained smaller than in 100 μM ADPR (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: AMPCPR-activated nvTRPM2 currents declined ~1.5 times faster than ADPR-activated currents upon nucleotide removal.
source: Upon nucleotide removal, AMPCPR-activated nvTRPM2 currents declined ~1.5 times faster than ADPR-activated currents (Figure 5B, colored fit lines and time constants; Figure 5D, p = 0.02), suggesting a somewhat destabilized open state for AMPCPR-bound channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: AMPCPR-bound nvTRPM2 channels have a somewhat destabilized open state.
source: Upon nucleotide removal, AMPCPR-activated nvTRPM2 currents declined ~1.5 times faster than ADPR-activated currents (Figure 5B, colored fit lines and time constants; Figure 5D, p = 0.02), suggesting a somewhat destabilized open state for AMPCPR-bound channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the faster deactivation kinetics.

claim: AMPCPR is a partial agonist for nvTRPM2.
source: Thus, AMPCPR is a partial agonist for nvTRPM2, just as for human TRPM2 (Tóth et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lower efficacy and faster deactivation of AMPCPR compared to ADPR.

claim: AMPCPR supports nvTRPM2 pore gating in the complete absence of nvNUDT9-H catalytic activity.
source: Nevertheless, it clearly supports pore gating in the complete absence of nvNUDT9-H catalytic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that AMPCPR activates channels but is not hydrolyzed.

claim: The double mutation E1443I/F1444L in nvNUDT9-H reduced kcat to ~1% of WT.
source: However, maximal turnover rate was dramatically impaired by both double mutations: kcat was ~1% of WT for E1443I/F1444L (Figure 6B, red bar), and ~0.1% of WT for E1446K/E1447K (Figure 6B, blue bar), consistent with the reported effects of the analogous mutations on the catalytic activity of human NUDT9 (Perraud et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The double mutation E1446K/E1447K in nvNUDT9-H reduced kcat to ~0.1% of WT.
source: However, maximal turnover rate was dramatically impaired by both double mutations: kcat was ~1% of WT for E1443I/F1444L (Figure 6B, red bar), and ~0.1% of WT for E1446K/E1447K (Figure 6B, blue bar), consistent with the reported effects of the analogous mutations on the catalytic activity of human NUDT9 (Perraud et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Full-length nvTRPM2 channels bearing the E1443I/F1444L or E1446K/E1447K double mutations generated macroscopic currents that were activated by low micromolar concentrations of ADPR.
source: Whereas enzymatic activity of nvNUDT9-H was nearly abolished by both double mutations, full-length nvTRPM2 channels bearing the same double mutations generated macroscopic currents that were activated by low micromolar concentrations of ADPR (Figure 6D–E), just as WT nvTRPM2 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Neither the apparent affinity for macroscopic current activation by ADPR nor the time constant of current deactivation upon ADPR removal were significantly affected by the E1443I/F1444L or E1446K/E1447K double mutations in nvTRPM2.
source: Neither the apparent affinity for macroscopic current activation by ADPR (K1/2 ~2 μM; Figure 6F), nor the time constant of current deactivation upon ADPR removal (τ ~100 ms; Figure 6C–E, colored lines and time constants; Figure 6G) were significantly affected by either double mutation (p > 0.17).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional analysis shown in Figure 6F-G.

claim: Mg2+ removal slightly accelerated nvTRPM2 channel gating, with both mean burst and interburst durations becoming ~30% shorter.
source: As expected from the macroscopic current measurements (Figure 4B–C, cf., Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), Mg2+ removal did not affect open probability of WT nvTRPM2 (Figure 7D, orange vs. green bar), although it slightly accelerated channel gating: both mean burst and interburst durations became ~30% shorter (Figure 7E–F, orange vs. green bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel kinetic analysis shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: For both E1443I/F1444L and E1446K/E1447K nvTRPM2 mutants, open probabilities and mean burst durations remained similar to those of WT.
source: Moreover, for both double mutants, open probabilities and mean burst durations remained similar to those of WT, and mean interburst durations were altered by less than twofold (Figure 7D–F, red and blue bars vs. green bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-channel kinetic analysis shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: All the subtle effects on single-channel gating parameters caused by the mutations or Mg2+ removal proved statistically insignificant.
source: All the subtle effects on single-channel gating parameters caused by the mutations or Mg2+ removal (Figure 7D–F) proved statistically insignificant (p > 0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical assessment of the data shown in Figure 7D-F.

claim: A key characteristic feature of human TRPM2 is a rapid inactivation process, even in the presence of its activating ligands.
source: A key characteristic feature of human TRPM2 (hsTRPM2) is a rapid inactivation process, even in the presence of its activating ligands (Csanády and Törocsik, 2009; Tóth and Csanády, 2012), which is not observed for nvTRPM2 (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inactivation is not observed for nvTRPM2.
source: A key characteristic feature of human TRPM2 (hsTRPM2) is a rapid inactivation process, even in the presence of its activating ligands (Csanády and Törocsik, 2009; Tóth and Csanády, 2012), which is not observed for nvTRPM2 (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Inactivation of hsTRPM2 reflects a conformational change of the pore.
source: Inactivation of hsTRPM2 reflects a conformational change of the pore (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), and is linked specifically to the amino acid sequence of its short three-residue post-filter helix which lines the extracellular pore vestibule: indeed, swapping the corresponding residues between nvTRPM2 and hsTRPM2 confers inactivation to the anemone channel but eliminates it from the human channel (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Swapping the post-filter helix residues between nvTRPM2 and hsTRPM2 confers inactivation to the anemone channel but eliminates it from the human channel.
source: Inactivation of hsTRPM2 reflects a conformational change of the pore (Tóth and Csanády, 2012), and is linked specifically to the amino acid sequence of its short three-residue post-filter helix which lines the extracellular pore vestibule: indeed, swapping the corresponding residues between nvTRPM2 and hsTRPM2 confers inactivation to the anemone channel but eliminates it from the human channel (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: In the external pore vestibule of nvTRPM2, the acidic side chains of D1041 and E1042 in the post-filter helix, and of E1046 and E1050 in the post-filter loop, form a double ring of negative charges.
source: In the external pore vestibule of nvTRPM2, the acidic side chains of D1041 and E1042 in the post-filter helix, and of E1046 and E1050 in the post-filter loop, form a double ring of negative charges (Figure 8A, red sticks).
evidence: This claim is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 8A.

claim: When the pore helices and pore loops of nvTRPM2 and hsTRPM2 are aligned, the axis of the post-filter helix of hsTRPM2 is rotated by ~10° relative to that of nvTRPM2.
source: Not only are those charges absent in hsTRPM2, but when the pore helices and pore loops of the two structures are aligned, the axis of the post-filter helix of hsTRPM2 is rotated by ~10° (counterclockwise, when viewed from the extracellular side) relative to that of nvTRPM2 (Figure 8A, right).
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The displacement of the hsTRPM2 post-filter helix is caused by the appearance of a proline (P983) at its N-terminal end.
source: This displacement of the hsTRPM2 post-filter helix is caused by the appearance of a proline (P983) at its N-terminal end (Figure 8A, blue sticks).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The residue triplet which forms the negatively charged post-filter helix in nvTRPM2 is intact and preceded by a phenylalanine in all invertebrates.
source: Interestingly, a sequence alignment of the pore regions of TRPM2 orthologs (Figure 1, left) reveals that these changes in pore sequence, responsible for inactivation of the human channel, also appeared between chordates and vertebrates: the residue triplet which forms the negatively charged post-filter helix in nvTRPM2 is intact (Figure 1, Post-filter helix, blue sequence motifs) and preceded by a phenylalanine in all invertebrates, but is replaced by an uncharged doublet (Figure 1, Post-filter helix, red sequence motifs) and preceded by a proline in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The post-filter helix residue triplet is replaced by an uncharged doublet and preceded by a proline in vertebrates.
source: Interestingly, a sequence alignment of the pore regions of TRPM2 orthologs (Figure 1, left) reveals that these changes in pore sequence, responsible for inactivation of the human channel, also appeared between chordates and vertebrates: the residue triplet which forms the negatively charged post-filter helix in nvTRPM2 is intact (Figure 1, Post-filter helix, blue sequence motifs) and preceded by a phenylalanine in all invertebrates, but is replaced by an uncharged doublet (Figure 1, Post-filter helix, red sequence motifs) and preceded by a proline in vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The glutamate side chain in the selectivity filter responsible for the very high Ca2+ preference of the nvTRPM2 pore was replaced by an uncharged side chain in vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, the glutamate side chain in the selectivity filter responsible for the very high Ca2+ preference of the nvTRPM2 pore (Zhang et al., 2018) was also replaced by an uncharged side chain in vertebrates (Figure 1, Filter, blue vs. red residues), lowering Ca2+ permeability.
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1 and structural/functional data from Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The replacement of the glutamate in the selectivity filter by an uncharged side chain in vertebrates lowered Ca2+ permeability.
source: Furthermore, the glutamate side chain in the selectivity filter responsible for the very high Ca2+ preference of the nvTRPM2 pore (Zhang et al., 2018) was also replaced by an uncharged side chain in vertebrates (Figure 1, Filter, blue vs. red residues), lowering Ca2+ permeability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of charged residues in Ca2+ selectivity.

claim: srTRPM2 currents remained stable for over the time course of an hour.
source: Currents generated by srTRPM2 channels (Figure 8B) remained stable for over the time course of an hour, just like nvTRPM2 currents (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8B.

claim: drTRPM2 currents inactivated in the maintained presence of ADPR+Ca2+.
source: In contrast, drTRPM2 currents inactivated in the maintained presence of ADPR+Ca2+ (Figure 8D) just like those of hsTRPM2 (Figure 8E), although for the zebrafish channel the rate of inactivation was an order of magnitude slower (Figure 8D–E, compare time constants of single-exponential fits, average τ was 655 ± 178 s (n = 12) for drTRPM2, and 29 ± 2 s (n = 4) for hsTRPM2).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The rate of inactivation for drTRPM2 was an order of magnitude slower than for hsTRPM2.
source: In contrast, drTRPM2 currents inactivated in the maintained presence of ADPR+Ca2+ (Figure 8D) just like those of hsTRPM2 (Figure 8E), although for the zebrafish channel the rate of inactivation was an order of magnitude slower (Figure 8D–E, compare time constants of single-exponential fits, average τ was 655 ± 178 s (n = 12) for drTRPM2, and 29 ± 2 s (n = 4) for hsTRPM2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of inactivation time constants from Figure 8D-E.

claim: The average inactivation time constant was 655 ± 178 s for drTRPM2.
source: In contrast, drTRPM2 currents inactivated in the maintained presence of ADPR+Ca2+ (Figure 8D) just like those of hsTRPM2 (Figure 8E), although for the zebrafish channel the rate of inactivation was an order of magnitude slower (Figure 8D–E, compare time constants of single-exponential fits, average τ was 655 ± 178 s (n = 12) for drTRPM2, and 29 ± 2 s (n = 4) for hsTRPM2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological data.

claim: The average inactivation time constant was 29 ± 2 s for hsTRPM2.
source: In contrast, drTRPM2 currents inactivated in the maintained presence of ADPR+Ca2+ (Figure 8D) just like those of hsTRPM2 (Figure 8E), although for the zebrafish channel the rate of inactivation was an order of magnitude slower (Figure 8D–E, compare time constants of single-exponential fits, average τ was 655 ± 178 s (n = 12) for drTRPM2, and 29 ± 2 s (n = 4) for hsTRPM2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electrophysiological data.

claim: The deleterious EF→IL substitution in the Nudix box appeared between chordates and vertebrates.
source: Sequence alignment of NUDT9-H domains of TRPM2 channel orthologs from unicellular flagellates to mammals (Figure 1, right) reveals that the deleterious EF→IL substitution in the Nudix box appeared between chordates and vertebrates: the Nudix box sequences of all invertebrates are canonical (Figure 1, right, blue sequences), whereas those of all vertebrates are vestigial (Figure 1, right, red sequences).
evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A stable pore is a general feature of invertebrate TRPM2 channels.
source: To address whether a stable pore is a general feature of invertebrate TRPM2 channels and inactivation a general feature of vertebrate channels, we sought to test this feature for an additional member in both groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that both srTRPM2 and nvTRPM2 have stable pores.

claim: Inactivation is a general feature of vertebrate TRPM2 channels.
source: To address whether a stable pore is a general feature of invertebrate TRPM2 channels and inactivation a general feature of vertebrate channels, we sought to test this feature for an additional member in both groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that both drTRPM2 and hsTRPM2 inactivate.

claim: Pore inactivation of TRPM2 channels may have emerged to provide an alternative mechanism for turning off channel activity in vertebrates.
source: It is therefore possible that pore inactivation of TRPM2 channels emerged to provide an alternative mechanism for turning off channel activity.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the evolutionary advantage of inactivation.

claim: An advantage of pore inactivation might be that it allows the time window of Ca2+ influx through TRPM2 channels to be regulated independently of the degradation time course of cytosolic ADPR.
source: An advantage of the latter mechanism might be that it allows the time window of Ca2+ influx through TRPM2 channels to be regulated independently of the degradation time course of cytosolic ADPR, which might have acquired additional functions as a signaling molecule in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the functional advantage of inactivation.

claim: ADPR might have acquired additional functions as a signaling molecule in vertebrates.
source: An advantage of the latter mechanism might be that it allows the time window of Ca2+ influx through TRPM2 channels to be regulated independently of the degradation time course of cytosolic ADPR, which might have acquired additional functions as a signaling molecule in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.
